We Americans have no idea when Brits and Aussies will say a word like "chance" with the vowel sound of "pond," because we use the same vowel as the one in "chants," which is like "hat." Cambridge tells me "dance" follows the pattern of "chance," with the "long o" sound, while "romance" doesn't, sounding largely like it does in American English. Which makes it odd when in "The King and I," in the song "Shall We Dance," the two words are made to rhyme: https://youtu.be/QgVPnWmUqd4?t=140 American production; what do you expect? Anyway, understandably, Brits and Aussies might be scratching their heads about the assertion that "chance" and "chants" sound the same, but of course, the NYT puzzle is an American production, too. But the overseas objections are due to the vowel sound. Americans complaining that they don't pronounce the two words alike baffle me. The American complaints are mostly that they pronounce the "t" in "chants," which of course is not present in "chance." I will posit that unless they are orating or anchoring the evening news, they are most likely not pronouncing that "t," or pronouncing it ever so slightly, while also inserting an intrusive "t" in "chance." What people think they say and what they actually say are often two different things. And even if they did pronounce the "t" in one and not the other, the two words are still pronounced practically the same. I think some (not all) people get stuck and nitpick the puzzle,
